title: October’s drone market: big orders, new factories and the deployment gap
description: October brought substantial counter-drone orders, new manufacturing plans and further commercial deployments. Across the industry, the question is becoming how quickly suppliers can turn demand into dependable operations.
coverAlt: Editorial illustration of drones above a radar installation and aircraft manufacturing facilities.

paragraphs.text: An €84 million radar contract in Poland and $729 million in counter-drone awards spanning the United States and the Gulf provided two of October’s clearest signals of demand. Weibel’s order supports Poland’s SAN programme. Raytheon’s awards cover components of its LIDS counter-drone system for the US Army, Qatar and Jordan. Both announcements concern equipment that must operate within a wider defensive network.

The contracts point towards a more demanding phase of competition. Demonstrating that a product works is one requirement. Supplying it reliably, connecting it to other equipment and keeping it operational are others. October’s developments suggest that these practical questions will increasingly determine which companies turn technical promise into lasting businesses.

sections.heading: Poland puts industrial capacity at the centre

paragraphs.text: Poland offered a particularly clear view of the manufacturing challenge. Kongsberg announced plans to invest more than €45 million in a Polish factory to produce and maintain counter-drone systems. The proposed facility would support SAN and potential future European customers, creating more than 100 long-term jobs, according to the company.

Weibel’s radar contract, announced on 27 October, was with Polish defence electronics company PIT-RADWAR. The Danish supplier described it as the largest order in its history. Its radars will provide detection, tracking and classification within SAN’s combination of sensors, command-and-control and countermeasures. The order marks progress in procuring one essential layer of the network.

For suppliers, the opportunity extends beyond winning the initial equipment competition. A buyer assembling a national capability needs products delivered in batches, supported locally and connected to systems from other manufacturers. Those requirements create openings for specialists, while making industrial partnerships central to delivery.

The same production question appeared at the larger end of the UAV market. On 23 October, General Atomics Aeronautical Systems announced Spirit Defense as a partner for FQ-42 Vengeance airframe production, following a US Air Force production contract awarded in June. GA-ASI presented the partnership as a way to expand manufacturing capacity and strengthen its production base.

Small interceptors and uncrewed combat aircraft have different missions and economics. Their manufacturers nevertheless face a common test: turning demand into repeatable output. Delivery schedules, production rates and fleet support will provide the clearest evidence of progress.

sections.heading: Software becomes part of the procurement story

paragraphs.text: Integration is another part of that test.

Reuters’ 8 October report on Dutch software company Intelic described a late-September demonstration connecting equipment from several suppliers. Its Nexus software combined information from radars, sensors and cameras. A reconnaissance drone helped verify the target, while a human authorised the interceptor launch. The report also identified an existing €30 million Dutch defence contract.

The example illustrates the commercial importance of connecting hardware. A defensive system must turn information from different devices into a timely decision. Buyers also need to know who maintains those connections, supplies software updates and takes responsibility when components fail to work together.

For investors assessing the sector, this expands the field beyond aircraft and interceptors. Software and integration companies can occupy an important position between equipment suppliers and the organisations operating their systems. The durability of that position will depend on customer adoption, interoperability and the ability to support changing hardware.

sections.heading: Civilian demand meets the permissions problem

paragraphs.text: October also brought evidence of demand beyond armed forces.

On 13 October, the European Commission announced an additional €130 million for drone and counter-drone measures at external borders, covering authorities in 16 EU member states and Norway. The programme includes surveillance, IT integration, training and cooperation between authorities. That funding creates procurement potential; individual supplier contracts will follow through implementation.

Private infrastructure operators face a more complicated operating environment. Reuters reported on 21 October that European governments were examining how utilities and other operators could take a greater role in countering drones. France had legislated in August, Germany was reviewing options, and Poland had authorised designated security units around critical energy infrastructure. Responsibility for damage caused during an intervention remained a difficult question.

That uncertainty matters commercially. An infrastructure operator can have a security requirement and a budget while still lacking a clear route to authorising a response. Detection, incident management and active countermeasures involve different responsibilities. Suppliers pursuing this market will need to fit into those procedures as well as demonstrate technical performance.

sections.heading: Startups need a route from testing to orders

paragraphs.text: For younger companies, operational validation remains an important step towards procurement.

NATO DIANA announced on 1 October that seven innovators from six allied nations had received capability-development contracts for operational experimentation. Separately, the NATO Innovation Fund’s president told Reuters that counter-drone capabilities were among its priorities as the existing €1 billion fund expanded its presence in Poland.

These developments address two recurring startup needs: access to realistic testing and access to capital. The next commercial hurdle is converting that support into repeat customers. Investors will need to examine the path between a successful experiment, a procurement decision and sustained production.

sections.heading: Delivery drones face their own execution test

paragraphs.text: Commercial delivery offered a more everyday example of deployment. Walmart and Wing launched drone delivery at seven stores around Charlotte during October, making selected small items available to eligible customers. The rollout expanded the service’s operating footprint, while leaving its local economics to be demonstrated through use.

The relevant questions are utilisation, reliability, staffing and cost per delivery. Each additional service area creates an opportunity to gather operating evidence—and a requirement to make the service useful enough that customers return.

Across defence and commercial aviation, October’s announcements put execution at the centre of the market. Factories, software connections, maintenance arrangements and operating permissions increasingly shape the value of an aircraft or counter-drone product.
The companies to watch next are those that can show the next measurable step: equipment delivered, systems connected, services used and customers placing another order.
